heading: One lot becomes two
paragraphs: On Monday afternoon, an assessor splits one lot into two. The parcel map, which shows every piece of land in a county and records who owns it, should now show both lots.

Five county offices use that map every day. The assessor sets property values, and planning reviews building permits. Public works maintains roads and pipes. Dispatch sends fire crews and ambulances, while the open data portal publishes the map to the public.
In the example county in “The Parcel Problem,” there are 48,212 parcels. The numbers are illustrative, but the question is concrete: when a parcel changes, which map shows it?

heading: Five copies, five schedules
paragraphs: Each office keeps its own copy. The assessor edits its map directly. Open data copies it nightly, dispatch weekly, and planning monthly. Public works updates its copy by hand.
Immediately after Monday’s split, only the assessor’s map shows it. Thirty days later, four maps show the change. One still doesn’t.

Even the parcel ID, the value that identifies a piece of land, has a different column name in each copy: Parcel_ID, ParcelNumber, PID, PARCEL_NO, and MapLot. Moving records between copies means accounting for those differences as well as their update schedules.

heading: A refresh replaces too much
paragraphs: Each copy is a hosted layer in ArcGIS Online, the online copy of a map that web maps and apps read.
The usual refresh overwrites the whole layer. It deletes and reloads every row, with each row representing a parcel. To carry a typical day’s 312 changes, it rewrites 47,900 unchanged rows too.
That approach also runs into a restriction. Offline sync, which lets field crews edit without a signal and send their work back later, prevents a hosted layer from being overwritten.

There are separate problems here. The county needs one official record instead of competing copies. Refreshes need to send only changes. Readers also need their own read-only outputs rather than sharing a layer with editors.

heading: One place to edit
paragraphs: The design starts with one database of record, the place that holds the official parcels.

Staff reach it through one editing service on ArcGIS Enterprise. The service is a door into the database, not another copy, so there is nothing to sync between them. The assessor works at a desk. Planning and public works use a web browser. Field crews use Field Maps, a phone app for map work, offline when needed.
The database records who made each change and when. Those stamps are called editor tracking.

Each office edits in its own version, a private draft of the record that nobody else sees yet. A field crew with no signal edits on the phone, and when the signal returns those edits sync into a draft too. The assessor's office reconciles each draft against the record and posts it. A parcel changed in two drafts is flagged for a person to decide, so one office never silently overwrites another. Only posted edits become the record.

heading: Only the changes move
paragraphs: At 2:00 am each night, an automated job asks the database what was added, edited or deleted since its last run.

It checks row counts, whether parcel shapes are valid, and whether column names match what the outputs expect. If a check fails, the run stops and yesterday's outputs stay live. Otherwise it publishes only the changes.
For the typical day shown, that means applying edits to 312 parcels, or 0.6 percent of the rows, in the hosted layer. Nothing is overwritten.

The same changes go into a GeoParquet file, a format that stores geographic records so analysts can query them directly. They also go into a PMTiles file, a format containing map tiles that web maps outside ArcGIS can draw.
Every office reads from these outputs instead of maintaining its own copy. Monday afternoon’s lot split appears on all five maps by Tuesday morning.

heading: Closing
paragraphs: Copies to keep in step fall from 5 to 0. Rows rewritten per refresh fall from 48,212 to 312, and places where a parcel can be edited fall from 5 to 1.
The result comes from separating editing from reading and giving changes a defined path between them.
A lot changes once in the official record. After review where needed and the nightly checks, every office can read that change without maintaining another map.
